q: What are the basic rules of basketball?
a: Basketball is played between two teams of five players each on a rectangular court with a hoop at each end. The objective is to score points by shooting the ball through the opponent's hoop. A field goal inside the three-point arc is worth 2 points, shots from beyond the arc are worth 3 points, and free throws are worth 1 point each. Players advance the ball by dribbling or passing — traveling (taking more than two steps without dribbling) and double dribbling are violations. Games are divided into four quarters (12 minutes in the NBA, 10 minutes internationally), and the team with the most points at the end wins. Fouls result in free throws or possession changes, and players are disqualified after accumulating a certain number of personal fouls (6 in the NBA, 5 internationally).

q: How does the NBA season work?
a: The National Basketball Association (NBA) is the premier professional basketball league in the world, founded in 1946. It consists of 30 teams divided into two conferences (Eastern and Western), each with three divisions. The regular season runs from October to April, with each team playing 82 games. The top eight teams from each conference advance to the playoffs, a best-of-seven elimination tournament. The conference champions meet in the NBA Finals, also a best-of-seven series. The NBA Draft allows teams to select eligible players annually, with the worst-performing teams receiving higher draft picks to maintain competitive balance. The league has produced iconic dynasties including the Boston Celtics, Chicago Bulls, Los Angeles Lakers, and Golden State Warriors.

q: What are the positions in basketball?
Point guard, shooting guard, small forward, power forward, center
What does each position do in basketball?
a: Basketball features five primary positions. The point guard (PG) is the floor general, responsible for directing the offense, handling the ball, and setting up teammates — known for passing and court vision. The shooting guard (SG) is typically the team's best outside shooter and perimeter scorer. The small forward (SF) is a versatile player who scores from various spots, rebounds, and plays defense against multiple positions. The power forward (PF) plays near the basket, focusing on rebounding, post scoring, and interior defense. The center (C) is usually the tallest player, anchoring the defense near the rim, blocking shots, and scoring from close range. In the modern NBA, positions have become more fluid, with positionless basketball becoming common.

q: Who are the greatest basketball players of all time?
Michael Jordan vs LeBron James vs Stephen Curry vs Kobe Bryant
GOAT debate in basketball: Jordan or LeBron?
a: The NBA has produced legendary figures who transformed the game. Michael Jordan won six championships with the Chicago Bulls, earning five MVP awards and widely considered the greatest of all time for his scoring, defense, and competitive drive. LeBron James, the NBA's all-time leading scorer, has won four championships with three different teams and is praised for his longevity, versatility, and basketball IQ. Kobe Bryant, a five-time champion with the Lakers, was known for his footwork, scoring ability, and 'Mamba Mentality.' Stephen Curry revolutionized basketball with his three-point shooting, winning four championships and two MVPs while changing how the game is played. Other all-time greats include Magic Johnson, Larry Bird, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Wilt Chamberlain, Bill Russell, Tim Duncan, Shaquille O'Neal, and Hakeem Olajuwon.

q: What is the shot clock in basketball?
How does the shot clock work?
Why was the shot clock introduced in basketball?
How many seconds on the shot clock in NBA?
a: The shot clock is a timer used in basketball to increase the pace of play and prevent stalling. In the NBA, teams have 24 seconds to attempt a shot that hits the rim, while college basketball (NCAA) uses 30 seconds for men and 30 seconds for women. The shot clock was invented by Danny Biasone and introduced to the NBA in 1954 after several low-scoring games, most notably a 19-18 contest between the Fort Wayne Pistons and Minneapolis Lakers. Before the shot clock, teams would hold the ball indefinitely once they had a lead. The innovation revolutionized basketball by increasing scoring and pace — average NBA scores jumped from around 79 points per game before the shot clock to 93 points after its introduction. If the shot clock expires before a shot is attempted, the opposing team gains possession.

q: How does the NCAA tournament work?
a: March Madness is the NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament, a single-elimination college basketball competition held every spring in the United States. It features 68 teams, with 32 automatic bids given to conference champions and 36 at-large selections chosen by a selection committee. The tournament is divided into four regions, and teams are seeded 1 through 16 within each region. The famous 'First Four' round reduces the field to 64, followed by the Round of 64, Round of 32, Sweet Sixteen, Elite Eight, Final Four, and the national championship game. The tournament is known for its unpredictability, Cinderella stories (lower-seeded teams making deep runs), and the popularity of bracket pools. The event generates massive attention and billions of dollars in advertising revenue.

q: How does basketball in the Olympics differ from the NBA?
a: Basketball has been an Olympic sport since the 1936 Berlin Games, with the United States dominating both the men's and women's competitions. The men's tournament features 12 teams competing in a group stage followed by a knockout round, using FIBA rules which differ slightly from the NBA — games are 40 minutes (four 10-minute quarters), the three-point line is closer, and defensive goaltending rules are different. The 1992 US 'Dream Team' featuring Michael Jordan, Magic Johnson, and Larry Bird is considered the greatest team ever assembled. The US men have won 16 gold medals, while the US women have dominated even more thoroughly with 9 gold medals (including seven consecutive from 1996-2020). Other strong basketball nations include Spain, Argentina, Australia, and France.
